subject: science
chapter_title: The World of Metals and Non-Metals

concepts.title: Physical Properties of Metals -- Lustre, Hardness, Malleability
concepts.definition: Metals are elements that have a shiny appearance (lustre), are generally hard, and can be beaten into thin sheets (malleable) or drawn into wires (ductile); they are good conductors of heat and electricity.
concepts.key_idea: Metals share characteristic physical properties -- lustre, hardness, malleability, ductility, sonority and good conductivity -- that distinguish them from non-metals.
question_patterns: What are the physical properties of metals?
What is malleability? Give an example.
Why do metals have a shiny appearance?
Which metal is the best conductor of electricity?
What is ductility in metals?

solution_steps.explain: Metals have a shiny surface (lustre) when freshly cut or polished and are generally hard (except sodium and potassium which are soft).
Metals can be hammered into thin sheets (malleability, e.g., gold and silver) and drawn into thin wires (ductility, e.g., copper).
Metals are good conductors of heat and electricity and produce a ringing sound when struck (sonorous).

worked_examples.question: Why is gold used for making thin foils for decorating sweets?
worked_examples.solution: Gold is highly malleable; it can be beaten into extremely thin sheets (foils) without breaking, which is why it is used to decorate sweets.
worked_examples.answer: Gold is highly malleable, so it can be beaten into very thin foils.

worked_examples.question: Why are copper and aluminium wires used for electrical transmission?
worked_examples.solution: Copper and aluminium are good conductors of electricity and are ductile, so they can be drawn into long wires that carry current efficiently.
worked_examples.answer: They are good conductors and ductile, making them ideal for wires.

exercises.question: List five physical properties of metals.
Define malleability and ductility with examples.
Why are metals good conductors of electricity?

concepts.title: Physical Properties of Non-Metals
concepts.definition: Non-metals are elements that are generally dull in appearance, brittle, non-malleable and non-ductile, and are poor conductors of heat and electricity; they exist as solids, liquids or gases at room temperature.
concepts.key_idea: Non-metals lack the properties of metals -- they are dull, brittle, non-conductors -- and can be solids (sulphur, carbon), liquids (bromine) or gases (oxygen, nitrogen).
question_patterns: What are the physical properties of non-metals?
Why are non-metals called brittle?
Name a non-metal that is a liquid at room temperature.
Are non-metals good conductors of electricity?
Give two examples each of solid, liquid and gaseous non-metals.

solution_steps.explain: Most non-metals (except iodine and diamond) have a dull, non-lustrous appearance.
Non-metals are brittle -- they break into pieces when hammered -- and are poor conductors of heat and electricity.
Non-metals can be solids (sulphur, phosphorus, carbon), liquids (bromine) or gases (oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen) at room temperature.

worked_examples.question: A piece of sulphur is hammered. What happens and why?
worked_examples.solution: Sulphur is a non-metal and is brittle, so it breaks into a powdery substance when hammered; it cannot be drawn into sheets like a metal.
worked_examples.answer: Sulphur breaks into powder because it is brittle.

worked_examples.question: Why is diamond classified as a non-metal even though it is hard and lustrous?
worked_examples.solution: Diamond is a form of carbon, a non-metal. Although it is exceptionally hard and can be lustrous, it is a non-conductor of electricity and is chemically a non-metal, so it is classified as a non-metal.
worked_examples.answer: Diamond is carbon (a non-metal); it is a non-conductor despite being hard.

exercises.question: List the physical properties of non-metals.
Name a non-metal that exists as a liquid at room temperature.
Why are non-metals poor conductors of electricity?

concepts.title: Chemical Properties of Metals -- Reaction with Oxygen, Water and Acids
concepts.definition: Metals react with oxygen to form basic oxides, with water to form hydroxides and hydrogen gas, and with dilute acids to produce salt and hydrogen gas; the reactivity varies from metal to metal.
concepts.formula: metal + oxygen -> metal oxide; metal + acid -> salt + hydrogen
concepts.key_idea: Metals are reactive elements that form basic oxides with oxygen, hydroxides with water, and salts with acids, releasing hydrogen gas in the latter two reactions.
question_patterns: What happens when metals react with oxygen?
Write the reaction of magnesium with oxygen.
How do metals react with dilute acids?
Which gas is produced when a metal reacts with an acid?
Why does sodium react violently with water?

solution_steps.action: Identify the metal and the reactant
solution_steps.explain: Note the metal (e.g., magnesium, zinc, sodium) and whether it reacts with oxygen, water or an acid.
Metal + O2 -> metal oxide (basic); Metal + water -> metal hydroxide + H2; Metal + dilute acid -> salt + H2.

solution_steps.action: Identify the products and their nature
solution_steps.explain: Metal oxides are basic, hydroxides are alkaline, and hydrogen gas burns with a pop sound; the salt formed depends on the acid used.

worked_examples.question: Write the balanced equation for the reaction of magnesium with oxygen.
worked_examples.solution: 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO. Magnesium burns in air with a dazzling white flame to form magnesium oxide, a basic oxide.

worked_examples.question: What happens when zinc reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid?
worked_examples.solution: Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2. Zinc displaces hydrogen from the acid, forming zinc chloride and releasing hydrogen gas which burns with a pop sound.
worked_examples.answer: Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2 (hydrogen gas is released)

exercises.question: Write the word equation for the reaction of a metal with oxygen.
Balance the equation: Mg + O2 -> MgO.
Why do sodium and potassium catch fire when dropped in water?

concepts.title: Chemical Properties of Non-Metals -- Reaction with Oxygen and Acids
concepts.definition: Non-metals react with oxygen to form acidic or neutral oxides; most non-metals do not react with dilute acids to displace hydrogen, unlike metals.
concepts.key_idea: Non-metal oxides are acidic in nature and turn blue litmus red; non-metals generally do not displace hydrogen from dilute acids.
question_patterns: What happens when non-metals react with oxygen?
Write the reaction of carbon with oxygen.
Are non-metal oxides acidic or basic?
Do non-metals react with dilute acids? Explain.
How does sulphur dioxide affect litmus paper?

solution_steps.action: Identify the non-metal and the reactant
solution_steps.explain: Note the non-metal (e.g., carbon, sulphur) and whether it reacts with oxygen or an acid.
Non-metal + O2 -> non-metal oxide; the oxide is acidic (e.g., CO2, SO2) and turns blue litmus red.
Most non-metals do not react with dilute acids to produce hydrogen because they cannot donate electrons easily like metals.

worked_examples.question: What is the nature of the oxide formed when sulphur burns in air?
worked_examples.solution: Sulphur burns in air to form sulphur dioxide (SO2), which is an acidic oxide. When dissolved in water it forms sulphurous acid, turning blue litmus red.
worked_examples.answer: SO2 is an acidic oxide that turns blue litmus red.

worked_examples.question: Why does carbon not react with dilute hydrochloric acid to produce hydrogen?
worked_examples.solution: Carbon is a non-metal and cannot donate electrons to the hydrogen ions in the acid, so it cannot displace hydrogen; hence no reaction occurs.
worked_examples.answer: Carbon is a non-metal and cannot displace hydrogen from dilute acids.

exercises.question: Write the word equation for the reaction of carbon with oxygen.
State whether non-metal oxides are acidic or basic.
Why do non-metals not displace hydrogen from dilute acids?

concepts.title: Reactivity Series of Metals
concepts.definition: The reactivity series is a list of metals arranged in decreasing order of their reactivity, with potassium being the most reactive and gold the least reactive metal.
concepts.formula: k > na > ca > mg > al > zn > fe > pb > cu > hg > ag > au
concepts.key_idea: The higher a metal is in the reactivity series, the more readily it reacts with oxygen, water and acids; a more reactive metal can displace a less reactive metal from its salt solution.
question_patterns: What is the reactivity series of metals?
Which is the most reactive metal?
Why is gold found in the free state in nature?
Can zinc displace copper from copper sulphate solution? Explain.
Arrange sodium, iron, copper and gold in decreasing order of reactivity.

solution_steps.action: Locate both metals in the reactivity series
solution_steps.explain: Find the positions of the two metals in the series K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au.
The metal placed higher in the series is more reactive than the one placed lower.
A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its salt solution; if the metal is lower, no reaction occurs.

worked_examples.question: Can iron displace copper from copper sulphate solution?
worked_examples.solution: Iron is above copper in the reactivity series (Fe > Cu), so iron is more reactive and can displace copper from copper sulphate solution: Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu.
worked_examples.answer: Yes, iron displaces copper because Fe is more reactive than Cu.

worked_examples.question: Why is gold found in nature in the free (native) state?
worked_examples.solution: Gold is the least reactive metal (at the bottom of the reactivity series), so it does not react with oxygen, water or acids and remains uncombined in nature.
worked_examples.answer: Gold is least reactive, so it does not combine with other elements and is found free.

exercises.question: Write the reactivity series of metals.
Will copper displace zinc from zinc sulphate solution? Give reason.
Name the most reactive and the least reactive metal.

concepts.title: Uses of Metals and Non-Metals
concepts.definition: Metals are used for making tools, machinery, wires, jewellery and construction materials due to their strength and conductivity; non-metals are used in fertilizers, water purification, medicines and as essential elements for life.
concepts.key_idea: The uses of metals and non-metals depend on their characteristic physical and chemical properties.
question_patterns: List five uses of metals in daily life.
How is copper used in electrical appliances?
What are the uses of non-metals?
Why is oxygen important for living beings?
How is chlorine used in water treatment?

solution_steps.action: Identify the property that makes the element useful
solution_steps.explain: Determine the relevant property -- e.g., conductivity of copper, malleability of gold, reactivity of chlorine.

solution_steps.action: Match the property to an application
solution_steps.explain: Relate the property to a use, e.g., copper's conductivity makes it ideal for wires; chlorine's reactivity makes it a disinfectant.
Describe how the element is applied in daily life, industry or biology.

worked_examples.question: Why is iron used in the construction of bridges and buildings?
worked_examples.solution: Iron is hard, strong and malleable; when mixed with small amounts of carbon to form steel, it becomes even stronger, making it ideal for construction.
worked_examples.answer: Iron is strong and malleable; as steel it is used in construction.

worked_examples.question: How is chlorine used in everyday life?
worked_examples.solution: Chlorine is a reactive non-metal used to disinfect drinking water and swimming pools by killing harmful microorganisms; it is also used in the manufacture of bleaching powder.
worked_examples.answer: Chlorine disinfects water and is used to make bleaching powder.

exercises.question: List three uses of metals and three uses of non-metals.
Why is aluminium used for making cooking utensils?
State two uses of non-metals in agriculture.

concepts.title: Corrosion of Metals
concepts.definition: Corrosion is the slow destruction of metals by the action of air, moisture or acids on their surface, forming oxides, carbonates or sulphides; rusting of iron is the most common example.
concepts.key_idea: Corrosion occurs when metals react with oxygen and water over time; it can be prevented by painting, oiling, galvanising or alloying.
question_patterns: What is corrosion of metals?
Why does iron rust?
What are the conditions necessary for rusting?
How can corrosion be prevented?
Why does copper turn green on exposure to air?

solution_steps.action: Identify the metal and the corroding agents
solution_steps.explain: Note the metal (e.g., iron, copper, silver) and the agents -- oxygen, water vapour, carbon dioxide or sulphur compounds.
The metal reacts with air and moisture to form a new compound on its surface, e.g., iron forms hydrated iron oxide (rust), copper forms basic copper carbonate (green layer).
Corrosion can be prevented by painting, greasing, galvanising (coating with zinc), tinning or alloying to keep air and moisture away from the metal surface.

worked_examples.question: Why does an iron gate kept in the open rust faster than one kept indoors?
worked_examples.solution: In the open, the iron gate is exposed to both oxygen and moisture (rain, humidity), which are the two conditions needed for rusting; indoors, it is protected from moisture, so it rusts slowly.
worked_examples.answer: Open exposure to oxygen and moisture speeds up rusting.

worked_examples.question: Why is galvanisation an effective method of preventing rusting?
worked_examples.solution: In galvanisation, iron is coated with a layer of zinc. Zinc is more reactive than iron, so it reacts with air first and forms a protective oxide layer, preventing iron from coming into contact with oxygen and water.
worked_examples.answer: Zinc coating protects iron by sacrificial protection and a barrier layer.

exercises.question: Define corrosion and give one example.
State two conditions necessary for the rusting of iron.
List three methods to prevent corrosion of metals.

concepts.title: Alloys and Their Uses
concepts.definition: An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of two or more metals, or a metal and a non-metal, prepared to enhance properties such as hardness, strength, corrosion resistance and low melting point.
concepts.key_idea: Alloys combine the desirable properties of their components to produce materials that are stronger, more durable or more corrosion-resistant than pure metals.
question_patterns: What is an alloy?
What is brass and what is it used for?
Why is stainless steel used for making utensils?
What is solder and why is it used?
How is an alloy different from a pure metal?

solution_steps.action: Identify the components of the alloy
solution_steps.explain: Note the metals (or metal and non-metal) that make up the alloy, e.g., brass is copper and zinc, steel is iron and carbon.
Describe how the alloy is superior to its components, e.g., harder, more corrosion-resistant, or lower melting point.
Relate the enhanced property to a practical use, e.g., stainless steel resists corrosion so it is used for utensils and surgical instruments.

worked_examples.question: What is stainless steel and why is it used for making cutlery and surgical instruments?
worked_examples.solution: Stainless steel is an alloy of iron with carbon, chromium and nickel. It is hard, corrosion-resistant and does not rust, making it ideal for cutlery and surgical instruments that need to be hygienic and durable.
worked_examples.answer: Stainless steel is corrosion-resistant and hard, ideal for hygienic uses.

worked_examples.question: Why is solder used for joining electrical wires?
worked_examples.solution: Solder is an alloy of lead and tin with a low melting point, so it melts easily when heated and solidifies to form a strong joint, making it ideal for joining electrical wires without damaging the components.
worked_examples.answer: Solder has a low melting point, so it joins wires easily without damage.
